settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The method does set XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, which many JAXP implementations use to restrict some entity expansion and external access.
getXMLReader() (lines 114-122) explicitly calls reader.setEntityResolver(IGNORING_SAX_ENTITY_RESOLVER), so the most common XMLReader path is hardened.
Class javadoc and method javadoc explicitly instruct callers to use OfflineContentHandler, indicating the delegation is intentional contract rather than an oversight.
getDocumentBuilderFactory() hardening shows the project is aware of and applies XXE mitigations on the DOM path; a parallel fix on the SAX path may be considered out of scope.
No caller of getSAXParser()/parseSAX() was read in this review, so actual reachability with an unhardened handler is unverified.
candidates.description: getSAXParserFactory() (lines 163-181) configures the factory as namespace-aware, non-validating, and sets XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING to true inside a try/catch that swallows ParserConfigurationException/SAXNotSupportedException/SAXNotRecognizedException. Unlike getDocumentBuilderFactory() (lines 193-206), which additionally sets external-general-entities=false, external-parameter-entities=false, load-external-dtd=false and load-dtd-grammar=false, the SAX factory does not disable external entity resolution at all. getSAXParser() (lines 139-147) returns such a parser without installing any EntityResolver, and parseSAX() (lines 326-337) hands it straight to parser.parse(is, contentHandler). XMLReaderUtils is a public, statically-callable utility, so any parser in the codebase (or downstream caller) that obtains a parser via XMLReaderUtils.getSAXParser()/parseSAX() and does not wrap its handler in org.apache.tika.sax.OfflineContentHandler or otherwise neutralize entities may be exposed to XML External Entity resolution (local file disclosure / SSRF against the XML processor) or entity-expansion denial of service when parsing attacker-supplied XML. The javadoc itself (lines 55-57, 130-132, 156-158) states that callers must wrap handlers in OfflineContentHandler, i.e. the safety is delegated and not enforced by the utility.
missing_evidence: Which parsers in tika-parsers actually call XMLReaderUtils.getSAXParser()/parseSAX() and whether each wraps its handler in OfflineContentHandler.
Whether getXMLReader() (or the OfflineContentHandler) is used exclusively in practice for untrusted input.
Behavior of the specific JAXP parser in use: whether FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING alone blocks external general/parameter entities on that implementation.
Any test (e.g. an XXE test) that would demonstrate or refute external entity resolution via this path.
preconditions: A parser (or library consumer) obtains a SAX parser through XMLReaderUtils.getSAXParser() or parseSAX() instead of getXMLReader()
The SAX handler used is not wrapped in org.apache.tika.sax.OfflineContentHandler
Untrusted XML content containing external entity / DOCTYPE declarations is parsed
The underlying JAXP implementation honors external entity resolution when FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING is set
candidates.title: XMLReaderUtils.getSAXParserFactory() enables SECURE_PROCESSING but does not disable external entities/DTD loading; XXE protection depends on callers using OfflineContentHandler

counter_evidence: All queue field accesses and swaps are guarded by SAX_READ_WRITE_LOCK / DOM_READ_WRITE_LOCK read/write locks, which limits (though does not eliminate) structural races and the documented NPE risk (lines 476-477).
releaseParser/releaseDOMBuilder explicitly document and tolerate the 'extra parser after resize' case ('will be gc'd'), so discarding is an anticipated, non-fatal outcome.
The waiting>3000 branch is a deliberate fail-safe intended to break permanent hangs rather than a normal path.
The default pool size is a fixed constant (POOL_SIZE = 10, line 71) and normal deployments never call setPoolSize().
candidates.description: setPoolSize(int) (lines 470-501) replaces the static SAX_PARSERS and DOM_BUILDERS queues with new ArrayBlockingQueue instances while holding only a write lock on the pool mutex, and it stores POOL_SIZE = poolSize at the very end after the queues have already been swapped. acquireSAXParser() (lines 410-437) and acquireDOMBuilder() (lines 347-374) poll the queue under a read lock, and after ~3000 iterations (a timer-based heuristic, not an exact count) call setPoolSize(POOL_SIZE) themselves (lines 366 and 429), i.e. a failing acquirer can trigger a pool replacement while other threads are mid-acquire/release. An in-flight parser/builder held by another thread will be offered back by releaseParser()/releaseDOMBuilder() (lines 381-399, 444-462) into a queue that may already have been replaced, producing the logged 'not taken back into pool' condition and silently discarding parsers. Additionally the size passed in is used directly to size the ArrayBlockingQueue ('new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(poolSize)'), so a zero/negative or otherwise out-of-range value supplied by an application embedding Tika (e.g. via XMLReaderUtils.setPoolSize) would throw or starve the pool; the public setter performs no range validation. The queue swap is a check-then-act on a static field, so the write lock protects the field assignment but not the assumption that the queue contents survive the swap.
missing_evidence: Whether any production code path calls setPoolSize() at runtime (as opposed to only application code during setup).
Whether the acquire wait loop's setPoolSize(POOL_SIZE) call can actually be entered under the write lock in a way that deadlocks or corrupts state (not demonstrated here).
Any bug report/test confirming pool-size values are expected to be validated, and the intended handling for zero/negative sizes.
Concurrency model of actual deployments (whether parses and setPoolSize run in parallel threads).
preconditions: Application (or a parser) calls XMLReaderUtils.setPoolSize() concurrently with parses that acquire/release SAX parsers or DOM builders
Or an acquire() waits long enough to hit the waiting>3000 branch and self-triggers setPoolSize(POOL_SIZE)
A caller passes an unvalidated/zero/negative pool size
candidates.title: XMLReaderUtils pool resize: setPoolSize() races with concurrent acquire/release and is called (with unvalidated size) from the acquire wait loop

counter_evidence: The path value comes from TemporaryResources / the JVM temp directory, which is normally operator- or OS-controlled, not supplied by the parsed document.

Execution is invoked via Runtime.exec(String) (no shell), so shell metacharacters such as ';', '|' or '$' would not be interpreted by a shell even if present; only argument splitting based on whitespace is a realistic concern.
This check runs only to detect whether the optional Python toolchain is present and is guarded/cached via temporary resources that are cleaned up in the finally block.
The remaining command-building logic of this parser (including any metadata interpolation) was not readable in this review.
candidates.description: hasPython() (lines 208-233) creates a temporary file via TemporaryResources, writes a Python import check into it, and then executes Process p = Runtime.getRuntime().exec("python " + importCheck.getAbsolutePath()) (line 220). The command is assembled as a single space-joined string, so if importCheck.getAbsolutePath() ever contained shell-relevant metacharacters or whitespace the string would be split by Runtime.exec(String) rather than treated as one argument; the temp path is produced by TemporaryResources (java.io.tmpdir based) and the read spans do not show it to be influenced by the parsed document or by request metadata. As written this looks like a robustness concern and a possible argument-splitting/quoting issue rather than an established injection. It is reported because (a) it is a command execution site reachable from OCR initialization/parsing of image input, and (b) the adjacent tesseract command construction (buildTesseractCommand, not within the read spans) is the conventional place metadata values are inserted into a command line, which is why the full parser body would need to be reviewed to confirm or refute injection.
missing_evidence: The full body of TesseractOCRParser (lines 320-700), in particular buildTesseractCommand / buildImageMagickCommand equivalent logic, to see whether document- or metadata-derived values are concatenated into the executed command line.
Whether TesseractOCRConfig values (tesseractPath, imageMagickPath, language) or request metadata reach any Runtime.exec / ProcessBuilder command string unquoted.
Whether the temp file name from TemporaryResources is derived from the uploaded document name or other untrusted input.
preconditions: Tesseract OCR parsing path is enabled and no Python dependency is already cached
The temp directory path (java.io.tmpdir) contains characters that Runtime.exec(String) mishandles, or an environment permits an attacker to influence the temp path
OCR parse is attempted on attacker-supplied image input
candidates.title: TesseractOCRParser.hasPython() builds a 'python <absolute path>' command string for Runtime.exec; path provenance from a TemporaryResources file (not established as attacker-controlled)
